Nwa Dị Mma

pronounced nwah dee m-MAH · Igbo for “the child is well”
A four-agent copilot that helps a health worker, birth attendant or family member in Nigeria recognise a pregnancy or childbirth emergency — in English, Pidgin or Igbo — and get the mother to a hospital that can save her, in time.

1 · Motivation: who has the problem

The context (for readers outside Nigeria). Nigeria has the highest number of maternal deaths of any country: roughly 29% of all maternal deaths worldwide — about one in four — at a ratio of 993 deaths per 100,000 live births in 20231, compared with about 19 in the United States. Worldwide, the leading causes are severe bleeding (27%) and pre-eclampsia/eclampsia (16%), followed by infection and obstructed labour2. Almost all of these deaths are treatable at a hospital that can operate and give blood — if the woman gets there in time. Only about 4 in 10 Nigerian births happen in a health facility3.

Why women don't get there: the three delays. The classic framework for maternal death4 names three delays. Nwa Dị Mma targets the first two:

1 · Deciding to goNot recognising a danger sign; waiting for a husband's permission; hoping it passes by morning.
2 · Reaching the right placeGoing first to a clinic or maternity home that cannot do a caesarean or transfusion, then being sent on.
3 · Receiving careStaff, blood and drugs at the hospital. Out of scope, but the handover note shortens it.

The person. A community health extension worker (CHEW), a traditional birth attendant, or a relative at a home birth in Enugu, Kano or Lagos. The woman has been in labour "since yesterday", or has "soaked three wrappers" after delivering at home, or has a headache "wey no gree" at eight months. The helper must decide, often at night: is this normal, or must she go now — and where? Conversations happen in English, Pidgin, Igbo, Hausa or Yoruba.

Current costs. Delay costs lives: postpartum haemorrhage can kill within hours. Going to the wrong facility costs time and money — a woman taken first to a small maternity home is referred on, often in a second hired vehicle. Over-referral has a cost too: a poor family pays transport and lost work for an unnecessary hospital trip, which teaches them not to go next time.

2 · What is new

Nwa Dị Mma is not a pregnancy chatbot. The AI agents do what language models are good at — reading messy Pidgin/Igbo/English descriptions, double-checking, explaining to the family in their language, writing a handover note. The decision itself (how urgent, where to go, which pre-referral medicine) is made by WHO danger-sign rules written as ordinary code, and a final check refuses any medicine or dose the code did not produce. Its distinctive move is choosing the right destination: an emergency goes to a hospital that can operate, not to the nearest clinic.

AlternativeWhat it does wellWhere it falls shortNwa Dị Mma's difference
Antenatal card / WHO danger-sign postersFree, trusted, offlineA list, not a decision; nothing about where to goApplies the same signs to the actual situation; names the hospital and distance
SMS reminder programmes (MomConnect-style)Reach many mothers cheaply; educationOne-way; no triage of a live emergency; no routingTwo-way: reads the description, decides, routes
Emergency transport schemes (community drivers in some states)Solve the vehicle problemSomeone still has to recognise the emergency and pick the destinationComplements them: decision + destination + handover note
ChatGPT / general chatbotsUnderstands free text; always availableNo protocol grounding; over-cautious and inconsistent; cannot name a real nearby hospital (measured below)Decision, destination and doses are deterministic code; 4 guards; real facility register

Measured head-to-head: Nwa Dị Mma vs. the same model asked directly

I asked the same model (gpt-6-luna) each of the 17 test cases the way a health worker might ask a chatbot ("Here is my note… what should we do?", with the same five urgency options) and scored its urgency against the WHO-rule answer and its medicines against the WHO pre-referral table (scripts/baseline_chatgpt.py).

Severe headache + blurred vision, 8 months (Igbo)emergencyemergencyemergency—

Baby not moving since yesterday (Pidgin)emergencyemergencyemergency—

Labour after a previous caesareanhospital nowhospital nowhospital now—
"Pregnant and not feeling well"needs infoneeds infoneeds info—

Total (16 cases; the direct-injection case is scored separately)12 / 1616 / 160 off-protocol

What the comparison shows. The plain model is safe but blunt: it never missed an emergency (0 under-triaged) and ignored the injected instruction. Its 4 misses were all over-cautious — normal labours sent to a hospital and no-danger-sign pregnancies told to go in today. Over-referral is not free: it costs a poor family a hired car and a lost day, crowds the few hospitals that can do caesareans, and teaches families to ignore the next warning. And a chatbot cannot say which hospital: Nwa Dị Mma names a real one from the GRID3 register, with distance and a handover note. It costs more per case ($0.0025–0.0029 vs. $0.0006), which buys four extra checks, three languages and the routing.

Honest limits of the comparison: the cases were written by me to cover the danger-sign rules, not sampled from real patients; 17 cases is small; the baseline is a single plain prompt; and the baseline was given no location, so it could not have named a facility.

3 · The agents

Organization

A sequential pipeline with guard rails between each agent (orchestrator in itoju/agents.py). In an emergency the order of checks must never change, so I chose a fixed pipeline over a free-form manager agent.

Each agent's role and tools

AgentRoleTools / outputWhy an LLM here
① IntakeTurn the description into 30 structured fields (stage, weeks, hours in labour, bleeding, headache, BP, baby moving, placenta out, risk factors…). Unknown = null, never "no".JSON validated by a Pydantic schema; one retry on invalid output; quotes the words behind each field.Descriptions mix English, Pidgin, Igbo and Hausa ("blood dey commot plenty", "isi na-awa ya nke ukwuu", "nakuda").
② Safety reviewerSecond opinion on the extraction, looking only for missed danger signs and wrong numbers.LLM review + deterministic English/Pidgin/Igbo danger-word net with negation handling. Can only escalate.A second, differently prompted read catches what the first missed; the code net catches what both miss.
③ ProtocolExplain the decision to the helper and to the family in English, Pidgin and Igbo.classify_case() and get_drug(name); tools read the verified findings server-side, so the model cannot pass in altered facts. Max 4 tool rounds.Clear, kind, short messages in three languages.
④ ReferralPick the destination; write an SBAR handover note and transport advice (blood donors, antenatal card).find_facility() over the GRID3 register: emergencies only to general/teaching/federal hospitals (caesarean-capable proxy); normal labour to the nearest birth facility. Names not in the register are removed.Weighing distance vs. capability; writing the handover.

Model choice

All four agents use gpt-6-luna, the only model allowed on the course key. It is fast and cheap (≈5.5 calls and ≈1.5 s of model time per case), which matters for a tool used at 2 a.m. on a basic phone. Because the clinical logic is in code, the model does not need medical expertise — it needs to read and write well in three languages. Tool-calling agents must use reasoning_effort="none" (a provider requirement); §4 shows that turning reasoning off for the two JSON agents too saves 13% with no accuracy loss.

One real run, traced step by step

Case (sample "Heavy bleeding after birth", Kano State, Nassarawa LGA): "Madam born for house 1 hour ago. Blood dey commot plenty, she don soak 3 wrapper, she dey weak and cold."

0
Input guard (code). No injection patterns → passed, 0 tokens.
1
Intake agent (1 call · 1,882 input tokens · 400 output). Pidgin → stage: after_birth ("born for house"), hours_since_birth: 1, vaginal_bleeding: true and heavy_bleeding: true ("blood dey commot plenty… soak 3 wrapper"), very_weak: true ("she dey weak"), each with its quote.
2
Safety reviewer (1 call · 507 input tokens · 233 output). Keyword net + LLM second opinion → "1 correction(s) made".
3
Protocol agent (2 calls · 1,976 input tokens · 404 output). Call 1: the model calls classify_case(); the WHO-rule engine returns emergency (heavy bleeding after birth), destination emergency hospital, actions (rub the womb, breastfeed, empty the bladder, arrange transport, bring two blood donors) and two pre-referral medicines from the table — oxytocin 10 IU IM or, if unavailable, misoprostol 800 micrograms — each "only if trained and available". Call 2: summary and family messages in English, Pidgin and Igbo.
4
Output check (code). Every medicine and dose in the agent's text matches the engine → passed.
5
Referral agent (2 calls · 1,629 input tokens · 210 output). Calls find_facility() from the centre of Nassarawa LGA; recommends Mohammed Abdullahi Wase General Hospital (2.3 km) over two primary health centres 1.4 km away because they cannot transfuse; writes the SBAR handover note and "bring blood donors" transport advice.

Total: 6 model calls · 5,994 input tokens (0 cached) · 1,247 output tokens · $0.0040 · 4.1 s of model time. (Numbers from the evaluation run; the screenshots show a separate run of the same case.)

Other runs

4 · Tokenomics

Every model call goes through one metered client (itoju/llm.py) that records input, cached-input, output and reasoning tokens from the API's usage field, plus latency and cost, to logs/runs.jsonl. The numbers below are measured: scripts/evaluate.py ran all 17 cases twice per configuration (34 runs each; 32 reach the model — the injection case is blocked for free).

Price assumption. I could not find published per-token prices for gpt-6-luna, so cost uses placeholder rates of $0.25 / 1M input, $0.025 / 1M cached input, $2.00 / 1M output, set in .env (PRICE_*_PER_M). Every dollar figure scales linearly with them; token counts are exact.

Per typical run (measured means, default settings)

AgentCalls / runInputCachedOutputof which reasoningCost / run
① Intake1.001,8791,72339681$0.00087
② Safety reviewer1.005070144107$0.00042
③ Protocol (3 languages)2.001,74203190$0.00107
④ Referral (75% of runs)1.501,18201300$0.00056
Total (default settings)5.505,3101,723990188$0.00292

Cache hit rate 32% of input tokens. Only the intake prompt (static instructions, Pidgin/Igbo/Hausa glossaries and an example) is long enough for automatic prompt caching (≥1,024-token prefix); static text comes first and the case note last so the prefix is identical on every run.

Cost-cutting experiment: reasoning off for the JSON agents

ConfigurationRunsCorrectOutput tok / runReviewer outputModel time / runCost / run
Default reasoning3434 / 349901441.5 s$0.00292
Reasoning = none (ITOJU_REASONING=none) — −13%3434 / 34802263.4 s$0.00254

Tradeoff: no measured loss of accuracy on these cases, 13% cheaper. Harder, longer descriptions might benefit from reasoning in the intake step; because the keyword net and rule engine back up the model, I would ship with reasoning off and watch the reviewer's override rate in the logs.

  • Referral agent only runs when she must go somewhere (75% of runs).
  • No LLM for decisions code can make — urgency, destination, doses and facility search are free and instant.
  • "Needs info" stops early; injection is blocked before any call — attacks cost $0.

Scaling: per user per month, 100 and 10,000 users

Assumption: one active helper (CHEW, midwife or birth attendant) checks 40 women per month — antenatal visits with a concern, labours and postnatal checks (≈2 per working day). Hosting: one small cloud VM (~$20/month) up to a few hundred users; ~$150/month load-balanced at 10,000 users.

ScaleCases / monthModel cost (default)Model cost (optimised)+ hostingTotal / user / month
1 user40$0.12$0.10—$0.10
100 users4,000$11.68$10.18$20$0.30
10,000 users400,000$1,168.00$1,017.60$150$0.12

Organization-wide view. A state programme with 10,000 helpers would spend about $14,011 per year on model and hosting at these prices — about $0.0025 per woman assessed. That is small next to one avoided late emergency, or one unnecessary hired-car trip that a correct "plan ahead" answer saves a family. The budget guard caps any single run at $0.05 and the deployment at a daily budget, so a bug or attack cannot create a runaway bill. Next saving: lengthen the protocol prompt's static prefix past 1,024 tokens so its two calls per run also hit the cache.

5 · Safety

Risks that matter for this app

RiskWhat could go wrongDefense built
Missed danger sign (under-triage)Intake misreads "isi na-awa ya nke ukwuu" or "placenta never comot" and a woman who must go now is told to waitReviewer agent + English/Pidgin/Igbo keyword net; both can only escalate
Invented facts / medicinesAI recommends a drug or dose outside WHO guidance (tranexamic acid, "misoprostol 1000 mcg to start labour", herbal "agbo")Medicines only from the WHO table, marked "only if trained and available"; output check blocks anything else and substitutes a safe template
Wrong action: wrong destinationSends a haemorrhage to a maternity home that cannot transfuse, or to a made-up facilityEmergencies routed only to general/teaching/federal hospitals; names not in the register removed
Guessing when data is missing"She's not feeling well" treated as fineUnknown stays null; engine returns needs_info with targeted questions
Prompt injectionText in the note tells the AI to recommend something or reveal keysInput guard blocks before any call; prompts treat the note as data; tools ignore model-supplied findings; output check
Infinite loops / overspendingA tool loop never ends; a bug runs thousands of callsMax 4 tool rounds per agent; 40k tokens and $0.05 per run; $2/day budget
Data leaksAPI key exposure; patient details sent elsewhereKey only in .env (git-ignored, verified absent from the repo); only the course model endpoint is called; notes logged locally only; helpers told not to enter names

Failures found while building — and fixed

  • Negation (over-triage): an early keyword net read "No chest indrawing" as a danger sign. Fixed with clause-level negation handling ("no bleeding", "she no dey bleed"); covered by the negations case.
  • Wrong destination: the first facility search picked an orthopaedic hospital, a bank staff clinic and a nursing school; GRID3 also labels many small private "specialist hospitals" as state-owned. Fixed by excluding unsuitable facilities and preferring general/teaching/federal hospitals within 25 km.
  • Over-strict guard: the facility check removed a correct hospital because the model appended "(2.3 km)" to its name. Fixed by matching register names inside the model's text.
  • Ambiguous Igbo: "ama jijiji" (trembling) was first mapped to convulsions; it also means shivering with fever, so I removed it to avoid false alarms.

Why this matters at scale (sourced)

  • Nigeria: ≈29% of global maternal deaths; 993 per 100,000 live births1. Bleeding and hypertensive disorders cause ≈43% of maternal deaths worldwide2 — exactly the emergencies where minutes and the right destination matter.
  • Only ≈4 in 10 births happen in a health facility3; at the rest, a relative or birth attendant is the only person who can start the referral.
  • Languages: family messages in English, Pidgin and Igbo — the languages a helper in the south-east actually uses with mothers and husbands.
  • Reach: the full GRID3 register covers 45,808 facilities in all 36 states + FCT5; the app runs in any phone browser at ≈$0.0025 per woman assessed.

7 · Limits and next steps

What doesn't work yet

  • Not clinically validated. 17 cases written by me; no real patient data; not reviewed by a Nigerian obstetrician, midwife or the NPHCDA. It must not be used for real patients before that.
  • No real capability data. GRID3 has no flag for caesarean section, blood bank or 24-hour staffing, so "can handle emergencies" is a proxy (general/teaching/federal hospitals). ~25% of sites have unknown functional status; distances are straight-line, not travel time at night.
  • Needs internet, and the decision is only as good as the description — the helper still has to look, ask and ideally measure blood pressure.
  • Medicines: only three WHO pre-referral options, only for trained staff; the app never replaces a midwife's judgement.
  • Language: Igbo messages still need review by more native speakers (dialects differ); Hausa and Yoruba are recognised as terms only; no voice input.
  • Prices for gpt-6-luna are assumed (see §4).

What I would build next

  1. Clinical review and a pilot with a state primary-health-care board and midwives: 200 real (de-identified) cases scored against senior midwives.
  2. Live capability map: hospitals mark "theatre open / blood available tonight", so routing uses real capacity, not a proxy.
  3. Transport hand-off: one tap to call a community emergency-transport driver with the destination and handover note.
  4. WhatsApp and voice notes in Igbo, Hausa and Yoruba; offline rules on the phone.
  5. Birth-plan follow-up: reminders in the last month of pregnancy and a postnatal check at 48 hours.
